UNIT GRID
Introduction
Reflections of KCF 2023
The three works in the unit ‘Beyond Fear’ —‘Little Hands, Big Courage’, ‘Everyday
Heroes’ and ‘The Trick of Kichu’ highlight the diverse and impactful nature of
heroism. They reveal that a hero isn't solely defined by grand, physical feats, but by
courage, quick thinking, and selfless action in moments of crisis. Whether it's a child
like Dilna bravely calls for help, the unseen dedication of everyday individuals and
working dogs, or Kichu the rabbit's clever use of intelligence, true heroes emerge
from a willingness to act for the well-being of others, often demonstrating that wit
and presence of mind can be just as powerful as strength in protecting and serving.
AF
The story ‘Little Hands, Big Courage’ strongly aligns with KCF objectives related
to Holistic Personal Development, National Consciousness and Responsible
Citizenship, Coping with Crises and Achieving Resilience, Knowledge Construction,
and Developing Critical Thinking. It also touches upon Self-Reliance as part of
Vocational Training and Self-Reliance.
The poem ‘Everyday Heroes’ strongly aligns with KCF objectives related to National
Consciousness and Responsible Citizenship and Coping with Crises and Achieving
Resilience. It also implicitly supports Holistic Personal Development and, to a minor
extent, Inclusive Education and Constitutional Values and Democratic Values.
‘The Trick of Kichu’ strongly aligns with KCF objectives related to Holistic
Personal Development, National Consciousness and Responsible Citizenship
(within a community context), Coping with Crises and Achieving Resilience,
Knowledge Construction (through application), and Developing Critical Thinking.
It also highlights Self-Reliance.
The picture story card strongly aligns with KCF objectives related to Inclusive
Education, Social Justice, and Holistic Personal Development. It also implicitly
supports Knowledge Construction, National Consciousness and Responsible
Citizenship, Constitutional Values and Democratic Values, and Developing Critical
Thinking.
All the genres included in this unit can be transacted effectively through IT assisted
techniques.

Deborah Lynn’s story highlights the vital importance of knowing how to act when

AF
Meet the author
Dilna and Isaac were playing when their mother suddenly fell. Eight-year-old
Dilna, though scared, remembered her grandmother’s advice. She bravely called
101, India’s emergency helpline. Dilna spoke clearly, giving her name and address.
Firemen quickly arrived and helped her mother, who soon recovered. The firemen
praised Dilna, calling her a hero. She later received an award for her courage. Dilna
was simply glad her mother was safe and decided to teach Isaac what to do in an
emergency.
Deborah Lynn
Deborah Lynn was born in New Orleans and spent her entire life in Baton
Rouge, Louisiana. As a young girl, Deborah Lynne dreamed of becoming an
actress one day. Later in life, She experienced life through the characters she
created in her books. Her first novel was published in 2007. Within 2 years,
3 more of her novels were released. Deborah has been a keynote speaker and
a guest speaker at several writers’ conferences, where she presented on many
topics, including Romance Writing, How to Get Published and The Do’s and
Don’ts of Writing.

Learning Objectives
Class IV
Introduction:
This unit revolves around the central theme of water, exploring its beauty, power
and essential role in sustaining life. Through sub-themes such as rain and rivers, the
unit highlights the importance of water in the natural world and in our daily lives.
The first lesson-, ‘The Journey of a raindrop’, takes us on a fascinating journey of
water in the form of a travelogue. Through the lively narration of water droplets,
learners witness a colourful picture of nature and the many creatures that depend on
water. The lesson reminds us how the earth eagerly awaits the rain and how a single
shower can bring about magical transformations in the environment. It emphasizes
not just the beauty of rain but also our responsibility to preserve and protect water.
AF
The second lesson, a poem titled ‘Where Go the Boats’, captures the imagination
of a child watching paper boats drift away. The poem gently explores the world of
dreams and hopes, showing how even a simple flowing boat can carry thoughts,
wishes and possibilities far and wide.
The third lesson, ‘Helping Cloud’, is a heartwarming story of various creatures
longing for rain. As they suffer from the heat and dryness, the arrival of the cloud
brings dramatic changes and relief.
“This story highlights how rain is essential for all living beings and shows how
water connects every form of life on Earth.”
Together, these three lessons invite learners to reflect on the value of water,
appreciate its many forms and develop a sense of responsibility to conserve this
precious resource. Water is not just essential for life — it also paints the world with
wonder, joy and hope.
Reflection of KCF-2023
The units clearly reflect the vision of the Kerala Curriculum Framework 2023
by promoting values such as environmental awareness, inclusiveness and social
responsibility. They encourage learners to observe nature with a scientific temper
and understand the role of water in sustaining life. The texts foster creative thinking
and critical analysis by presenting imaginative yet thought-provoking contexts.
Inclusiveness is emphasized as rain is portrayed as a blessing for all living beings,
without discrimination. The importance of hard work is subtly woven through the
perseverance of characters awaiting the rain. Most importantly, the units instill a
strong sense of social responsibility, urging learners to preserve water and actively
participate in cleaning and protecting their surroundings and natural resources, in
line with the goals of sustainable and value-based education promoted by KCF-2023.

Justification for the Title “Where Go the Boats?”
The title “Where Go the Boats?” may seem grammatically incorrect at first glance.
In everyday English, we would say, “Where do the boats go?” — using the auxiliary
verb “do” to form a proper question.
However, in poetry, language follows rhythm, sound, and style, not just grammatical
rules. The poet, Robert Louis Stevenson, uses an inverted sentence structure, a
common poetic device, to create a gentle, flowing rhythm that suits the mood of
the poem.
This inversion (“Where go the boats?”) sounds more musical and timeless. It also

reflects a childlike curiosity and wonder, as the poem explores the image of paper
boats sailing away into the unknown. So, while it doesn’t follow standard grammar,
it’s a creative and intentional poetic choice that enhances the beauty and emotion
of the poem.

use only scripts and vocal expression to help the audience understand the story.

‘story theatre’.)
